title: What does `System.exit(int status)` do (terminates the JVM, runs shutdown hooks but NOT `finally` blocks of still-running threads), why should it never appear in library/framework code, and what are exit codes (0 = success, non-zero = error)?

s1_definition.profdef: `System.exit(int status)` initiates JVM shutdown by calling `Runtime.getRuntime().exit(status)`. It runs all registered shutdown hooks and finalizers, then terminates the entire Java Virtual Machine, returning the given status code to the operating system. Crucially, it does not unwind the stack, so pending `finally` blocks and `catch` clauses of still-running threads never execute. The status code is an exit code where zero conventionally means success and any non-zero value means an error, and these codes are what calling processes, shell scripts, and orchestrators inspect to decide what happened.
s1_definition.analogy: `System.exit` is like pulling the master power switch on the entire bank branch. Everything stops instantly. The shutdown hooks are the small set of emergency routines wired to that switch, like locking the vault door, that do run as the power dies. But the tellers who were midway through counting cash do not get to finish or put the money back, because their careful cleanup steps, the `finally` blocks, are simply cut off. The exit code is the note left on the door for head office: a zero note means "closed normally," and any other number means "closed because something went wrong."
s1_definition.oneliner: `System.exit` kills the whole JVM, runs shutdown hooks but skips running threads' `finally` blocks, and returns an exit code where zero is success and non-zero is failure.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `System.exit(int status)` initiates JVM shutdown by calling `Runtime.getRuntime().exit(status)`. It runs all registered shutdown hooks and finalizers, then terminates the entire Java Virtual Machine, returning the given status code to the operating system. Crucially, it does not unwind the stack, so pending `finally` blocks and `catch` clauses of still-running threads never execute. The status code is an exit code where zero conventionally means success and any non-zero value means an error, and these codes are what calling processes, shell scripts, and orchestrators inspect to decide what happened.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** `System.exit` is like pulling the master power switch on the entire bank branch. Everything stops instantly. The shutdown hooks are the small set of emergency routines wired to that switch, like locking the vault door, that do run as the power dies. But the tellers who were midway through counting cash do not get to finish or put the money back, because their careful cleanup steps, the `finally` blocks, are simply cut off. The exit code is the note left on the door for head office: a zero note means "closed normally," and any other number means "closed because something went wrong."

**One line to remember:** `System.exit` kills the whole JVM, runs shutdown hooks but skips running threads' `finally` blocks, and returns an exit code where zero is success and non-zero is failure.

sections.s2_technical:
Calling `System.exit(status)` is a request to stop the entire JVM process, not just the current thread or method. Internally it delegates to `Runtime.getRuntime().exit(status)`, which begins the orderly shutdown sequence. First the JVM runs every shutdown hook you registered, where a shutdown hook is a thread you hand to `Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() -> ...))`. These hooks run concurrently and are the proper place for last-chance cleanup like flushing logs or closing a connection pool. After the hooks complete, the JVM halts and hands the status code to the operating system.

The behaviour that surprises many developers is what does not happen. `System.exit` does not throw an exception and does not unwind the call stack, so any `finally` block in a method that is currently executing on any thread will not run. For example, if a thread is inside a try-finally that would close a file, and another thread calls `System.exit`, that file-closing `finally` is skipped. The only cleanup that runs is the shutdown hooks. This is why relying on `finally` for critical cleanup is unsafe if `System.exit` might be called.

Exit codes are the integer the process returns to whoever launched it. By strong convention zero means success and any non-zero value means some kind of failure, and scripts depend on this. In bash you read it as the special variable dollar-question-mark, so `java -jar settle.jar; echo $?` prints the code. A deliberate example: a batch job might end with `System.exit(0)` on full success, `System.exit(1)` for a generic failure, and `System.exit(2)` for a specific condition like "some records were rejected," letting the surrounding shell or scheduler branch on the number. Container orchestrators like Kubernetes also inspect the exit code to decide whether to restart a crashed pod.

Now the central rule: `System.exit` must never appear in library or framework code. A library does not own the process; the application that imports it does. If a logging library or a date utility called `System.exit` because it hit a bad argument, it would kill the entire host application, including unrelated work like in-flight customer transactions, with no chance for the application to recover or respond gracefully. A library's job is to signal a problem by throwing an exception and letting the caller decide what to do. Only the top-level application entry point, the `main` method or a dedicated launcher, has the authority to decide the process should end.

There are further senior-level hazards. Because `System.exit` terminates the JVM, calling it inside a web request handler would take down the whole server for every user, not just the one request. Calling it inside a unit test can kill the test runner mid-suite. It also interacts badly with a `SecurityManager` in legacy systems, and in modern code the preferred patterns are to throw a domain exception upward, or in a true command-line tool to compute the intended exit code, return it up to `main`, and call `System.exit` exactly once there. If you truly must stop immediately without any hooks, `Runtime.getRuntime().halt(status)` exists, but it is even more abrupt and is reserved for genuine emergencies.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India our customers are Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001 holding ten lakh rupees, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001 holding two lakh fifty thousand rupees.

Problem 1 — we run a nightly settlement batch as a standalone command-line program, and our scheduler needs to know whether the batch succeeded so it can either proceed to the next job or raise an alert. We want the batch to end with a clean exit code: zero when every transfer settled, and a specific non-zero code when some were rejected, so the shell script around it can branch correctly.

Problem 2 — a developer once put a `System.exit` inside a reusable validation helper so it could "stop everything on bad input." When that helper was later reused inside our always-on transfer web service, a single bad request killed the entire server and dropped every other customer's in-flight transaction. We want to show the right way: the helper throws an exception, and only the top-level batch launcher decides the exit code, while a shutdown hook flushes our audit log so nothing is lost even on exit.

Our runnable demo will define an `Account` with debit and credit, a `SettlementValidator` that throws on bad input instead of exiting, a `SettlementBatch` that processes a list of transfers and computes a result, and a `main` that registers a shutdown hook to flush the audit log, runs the batch, and calls `System.exit` exactly once with the correct code. We will log what the shutdown hook does and what a skipped `finally` would have done.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/batch/*.java

# Run, then read the exit code the scheduler cares about
java -cp out com.bank.batch.SettlementBatchDemo
echo "Exit code was: $?"      # prints 2 here (one transfer was rejected)

# A shell script branching on the code
java -cp out com.bank.batch.SettlementBatchDemo
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "proceed to next job"; else echo "raise alert"; fi
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, 1000000), Priya (CUR3001, 250000), and three transfer rows — 50000 SAV2001 to CUR3001 (valid), -10 SAV2001 to CUR3001 (invalid amount), and 20000 CUR3001 to SAV2001 (valid).

Step 1 — at startup the demo registers a shutdown hook whose job is to flush the audit log. This hook is parked, waiting, and will run when the JVM shuts down.

Step 2 — the batch processes the first transfer. The validator accepts it, Rajesh is debited 50000 to 950000, and Priya is credited 50000 to 300000. Success is logged.

Step 3 — the batch processes the second transfer. The validator throws because the amount -10 is not positive. Note it throws rather than exiting, so the batch simply catches it, increments the rejected count to one, logs a warning, and continues. Had the validator called `System.exit`, the whole batch would have died here.

Step 4 — the batch processes the third transfer. The validator accepts it, Priya is debited 20000 to 280000, and Rajesh is credited 20000 to 970000. Success is logged. The batch returns a rejected count of one.

Step 5 — back in `main`, because the rejected count is non-zero, the exit code is chosen as 2, meaning partial rejection. The demo calls `System.exit(2)`. The JVM runs the shutdown hook, which logs that the audit log was flushed, and then terminates, handing 2 to the operating system where the shell reads it as dollar-question-mark.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-30 19:27:11 INFO    Settled 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001
2026-10-30 19:27:11 WARNING Rejected SAV2001→CUR3001: Amount must be positive, was -10
2026-10-30 19:27:11 INFO    Settled 20000 from CUR3001 to SAV2001
2026-10-30 19:27:11 INFO    Rajesh=970000 Priya=280000
2026-10-30 19:27:11 INFO    Rejected count: 1
2026-10-30 19:27:11 INFO    Exiting with code 2 (0=success, 2=partial reject)
2026-10-30 19:27:11 INFO    Shutdown hook: audit log flushed to disk
Exit code was: 2
```

```text
  Scheduler launches: java -jar settle.jar
    │
    ▼
  main(): register shutdown hook (flush audit log) ──parked──┐
    │                                                        │

  SettlementBatch.process(transfers)                         │

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
System.exit takes an integer status and initiates shutdown of the entire Java Virtual Machine, not just the current thread. Internally it calls Runtime.getRuntime().exit, which runs all registered shutdown hooks and then terminates the process, handing the status code back to the operating system. The behaviour that catches people out is that it does not unwind the stack, so the finally blocks and catch clauses of any threads that are still running do not execute. The only cleanup that runs is the shutdown hooks, which is why I register critical last-chance work like flushing the audit log as a shutdown hook rather than trusting a finally block.

Exit codes are the number the process returns to whoever launched it, and by strong convention zero means success while any non-zero value means an error. Shell scripts read this through the dollar-question-mark variable, and orchestrators like Kubernetes inspect it to decide whether to restart a container. I use distinct non-zero codes to mean distinct outcomes, for example one for a generic failure and two for a partial result where some records were rejected, so the surrounding scheduler can branch intelligently.

The rule I never break is that System.exit must never appear in library or framework code. A library does not own the process; the application that imports it does. If a shared helper called System.exit on bad input, it would kill the entire host application, including completely unrelated work, with no chance to recover. A library's job is to throw an exception and let the caller decide. Only the top-level entry point, the main method or a dedicated launcher, has the authority to end the process, and it should call System.exit exactly once after computing the right code.

At National Bank of India this bit us directly. A developer put System.exit inside a reusable validation helper so it could stop on bad input, and when that helper was later reused inside our always-on transfer web service, a single malformed request killed the whole server and dropped every other customer's in-flight transaction. We fixed it by making the validator throw an exception instead, and we kept System.exit only in the standalone settlement batch's main method, where it computes a clean exit code, zero when everything settled and two when some transfers were rejected, so our scheduler knows whether to proceed or raise an alert. We also register a shutdown hook there to flush the audit log, because once System.exit is called the running threads' finally blocks will not run, and we cannot afford to lose audit records.

---

keyPoints: Terminates the JVM immediately with the given exit code
Shutdown hooks run (if registered), but finally blocks may NOT complete
Never use System.exit() in library code — only in main application entry points
In tests: System.exit() kills the test runner — use SecurityManager to trap it
